keyTakeaways: ¡Feliz Halloween! works in every Spanish-speaking country; the verb ending (tienes, tenés, tenéis, tiene) is what marks a message as Mexican, Rioplatense, Spanish or formal.

faqs.question: How do you say happy Halloween in Spanish?
faqs.answer: Say ¡Feliz Halloween!, which is understood across Spain, Latin America and US Latino homes. ¡Feliz Noche de Brujas! (Happy Night of Witches) is a fully Spanish alternative, and FundéuRAE capitalises both Halloween and Noche de Brujas.

faqs.question: How do you say trick or treat in Spanish?
faqs.answer: FundéuRAE's October 2025 style note calls truco o trato the most established translation, with dulce o truco also in use. In Mexico, children instead go out to pedir calaverita.

faqs.question: Should I use tú or usted when wishing my boss a happy Halloween?
faqs.answer: Use usted unless your boss already speaks to you with tú and expects it back. A safe usted line is "Que tenga un feliz Halloween", which uses the third-person verb tenga.

faqs.question: How would an Argentinian friend word a Halloween text?
faqs.answer: With voseo: vos instead of tú, and verbs like tenés, sos and vení. "¡Feliz Halloween! Pasala bárbaro, te lo merecés" is a typical casual shape; have a Rioplatense speaker check anything longer.

faqs.question: Is Día de Muertos on the same day as Halloween?
faqs.answer: No. Halloween is 31 October, while Día de Muertos is 1–2 November: Sunday–Monday in 2026 and Monday–Tuesday in 2027. UNESCO lists the Mexican festivity as intangible heritage, inscribed in 2008.

faqs.question: Can I say Feliz Día de Muertos to a Mexican friend?
faqs.answer: Many people use it for 1–2 November, but the days are about remembering the dead. If your friend lost someone recently, a quieter line such as "Pienso en ti y en los tuyos este 2 de noviembre" is kinder.

faqs.question: Is jálogüin a real Spanish word?
faqs.answer: Not in the Real Academia's dictionary: a DLE search on 14 October 2026 returned that the word is not in the Diccionario. Write Halloween with a capital H, in roman type, as FundéuRAE advises.

faqs.question: Do Spaniards use vosotros in Halloween messages to a group?
faqs.answer: Yes. In Spain a group message uses vosotros forms such as pasadlo or venís, while Latin America uses ustedes for any group, formal or not.

faqs.question: What is a sweet Spanish Halloween text for a child?
faqs.answer: Keep it short and gentle, for example "¡Que tengas una noche de dulces y risas!" (Have a night of sweets and laughs!). Use tú with children and skip anything about blood or real fear.

faqs.question: Can I write the SubhSandesh Halloween card in Spanish?
faqs.answer: Yes, your own text can be Spanish: the letter, the word carved on the pumpkin and the closing question, which is editable up to 60 characters. The buttons and screens of both templates stay in English.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Wishes in Spanish: 32 Mensajes for Tú, Vos and Usted

Most Halloween wishes in Spanish start with *¡Feliz Halloween!* (feh-LEES ah-loh-WEEN), which works from Madrid to Los Angeles. What changes is the "you": *tú* for close people and kids, *usted* for a boss or an elder, *vos* in Argentina and Uruguay, *vosotros* for a group in Spain. Brevity wins, since 48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone and 90.9% of started pages are published and shared.

Below are 32 original *feliz Halloween mensajes* with English glosses, sorted by register and region, plus spelling, the Día de Muertos dates and when to skip one. Have a native speaker check any line that matters.

## How do you write "Feliz Halloween" correctly?

Write *Halloween* with a capital H, in roman type, without quotation marks. That is the ruling in [FundéuRAE's Halloween style note of 31 October 2025](https://www.fundeu.es/recomendacion/halloween/), which glosses the word as the contraction of *All Hallows' Eve*, the eve of All Saints' Day. It also capitalises *Noche de Brujas* and *Día de (los) Muertos*, and calls *truco o trato* the most established "trick or treat", with *dulce o truco* also used.

The hispanised *jálogüin* is not in the Real Academia's dictionary: a [DLE search on 14 October 2026](https://dle.rae.es/j%C3%A1log%C3%BCin) returned "La palabra «jálogüin» no está en el Diccionario". Keep the English spelling.

## Tú, usted, vos or vosotros: which "you" fits a Halloween wish?

Spanish has four everyday ways to say "you", and the wrong one reads as cold or cheeky. Mirror the form this person already uses with you; 31 October is no reason to change it.

The variety is younger than it looks. Linguist Víctor Lara Bermejo argues in [*Pragmalingüística* (December 2022)](https://revistas.uca.es/index.php/pragma/article/view/8266) that today's mix of *tuteo*, *voseo* and *ustedeo* took shape at the end of the 1700s and above all in the 1800s, for the same reasons in Spain and the Americas (abstract read only).

Regional pride is real. In a [2026 matched-guise study of Uruguayan Spanish](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13358585), 82 raters in Montevideo and 75 in Rocha judged *tú* and *vos* recordings. Montevideo heard pure *vos* as most Uruguayan; in Rocha, *tú* held a quieter local prestige.

## 32 Halloween wishes in Spanish, by recipient

Each group names its register first. Glosses are loose, because literal English kills the joke.

### 1. Short texts for anyone (no "you" needed)

These four avoid verbs that reveal tú or usted. They suit neighbours and mixed chats.

- "¡Feliz Halloween! Que esta noche solo asusten las películas." (Happy Halloween! May only the films be scary tonight.)
- "Dulces de sobra y ni un solo sobresalto." (Sweets to spare and not a single jump-scare.)
- "¡Feliz Noche de Brujas! Escobas listas a las ocho." (Happy Night of Witches! Brooms ready at eight.)
- "Abrazos de calabaza para todo el edificio." (Pumpkin hugs for the whole building.)

### 2. For a partner (tú)

Use *tú* forms such as *eres* and *tienes*. All five stay sweet rather than racy.

- "Contigo hasta los fantasmas me parecen buena compañía." (With you, even ghosts seem like good company.)
- "Este 31 no necesito disfraz: contigo puedo ser yo." (This 31st I need no costume: with you I can be me.)
- "Si esta noche se cruza un gato negro, que sea camino a tu casa." (If a black cat crosses my path tonight, may it be on the way to yours.)
- "Si grito en la película, abrázame y finge que no oíste nada." (If I scream at the film, hug me and pretend you heard nothing.)
- "Feliz Halloween, amor. Que sea el primero de muchos juntos." (Happy Halloween, love. May it be the first of many together.)

### 3. For friends in Argentina or Uruguay (vos)

*Voseo* changes the verb: *tenés*, *sos*, *vení*. These four use *caramelos* for sweets, the common Rioplatense word.

- "¡Feliz Halloween! Pasala bárbaro, te lo merecés." (Happy Halloween! Have a great time, you deserve it.)
- "¿Tenés planes para el 31? Vení disfrazado, sin excusas." (Got plans for the 31st? Come in costume, no excuses.)
- "Si te cruzás un fantasma, decile que va de mi parte." (If you run into a ghost, tell it I sent it.)
- "Que te sobren caramelos y te falten sustos." (May you have sweets to spare and frights to miss.)

### 4. For a group in Spain (vosotros)

Only Spain uses *vosotros* day to day; Latin America says *ustedes* for any group. These four suit a family or flat-share chat.

- "¡Feliz Halloween a todos! Pasadlo de miedo." (Happy Halloween, everyone! Have a frightfully good time.)
- "Que os toquen más golosinas que sustos." (May you get more sweets than scares.)
- "¿Venís disfrazados o tengo que asustaros yo?" (Coming in costume, or must I scare you myself?)
- "Esta noche os espero con castañas y una manta." (Tonight I'll be waiting with chestnuts and a blanket.)

### 5. For a boss, teacher or older relative (usted)

*Usted* takes the third-person verb: *tenga*, *disfrute*. Some families also use it with grandparents, so follow theirs.

- "Le deseo un feliz Halloween y un tranquilo Día de Todos los Santos." (Wishing you a good Halloween and a calm All Saints' Day.)
- "Que disfrute la noche con su familia." (Enjoy the night with your family.)
- "Profesora, gracias por su paciencia con una clase llena de monstruos." (Miss, thanks for putting up with a room full of monsters.)
- "Abuela, le guardé los mejores dulces de mi bolsa." (Grandma, I saved you the best sweets from my bag.)
- "Don Ramón, gracias por decorar el portal. ¡Que tenga un feliz Halloween!" (Mr Ramón, thanks for decorating the entrance. Have a happy Halloween!)

### 6. For kids (tú)

These five are short, silly and fine for a first-grader. None mentions blood or real fear.

- "¡Feliz Halloween, pequeño monstruo!" (Happy Halloween, little monster!)
- "¿Qué vas a ser este año: bruja, vampiro o calabaza?" (Witch, vampire or pumpkin: which one this year?)
- "Ningún fantasma del barrio sonríe como tú." (No ghost on the street smiles like you.)
- "Que tu calabaza brille más que la luna." (May your pumpkin shine brighter than the moon.)
- "Te reto a contar tus dulces sin comerte ninguno." (I dare you to count your sweets without eating one.)

### 7. Spanglish for US Latino families

In bilingual homes, mixing languages is normal and warm. These five use *tú* or no verb at all.

- "Happy Halloween, mija. Guárdale un dulce a tu abuelita." (…Save a sweet for your grandma.)
- "Trick or treat con los primos, y luego todos a casa de la tía." (…with the cousins, then everyone to auntie's.)
- "Happy Halloween from our casa to yours."
- "Mamá, you're still the scariest when I forget to call. ¡Feliz Halloween!"
- "Costume ready, abuela approved. ¡Feliz Halloween!"

## Which form to use where: a regional comparison

The table compares four Spanish-speaking audiences. Each row shows the verb form that gives a writer away.

| Region | Informal "you" | "You have" | Group "you" | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mexico | tú | tienes | ustedes | Día de Muertos on 1–2 November |
| Spain | tú | tienes | vosotros (tenéis) | Día de Todos los Santos on 1 November |
| Argentina and Uruguay | vos (tú also in Uruguay) | tenés | ustedes | Uruguayan listeners hear tú vs vos as regional |
| US Latino homes | tú, usted with elders | tienes | ustedes | Spanglish is fine; ask about family custom |

The greeting travels; the verb ending does not. *Tenés* sent to Madrid or *tenéis* to Mexico City marks an outsider.

## Which greeting for 31 October, and which for 1–2 November?

These are separate occasions. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027; Día de Muertos runs 1–2 November, Sunday–Monday in 2026 and Monday–Tuesday in 2027.

Día de Muertos sits on [UNESCO's Representative List of intangible heritage](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/indigenous-festivity-dedicated-to-the-dead-00054), proclaimed in 2003 and inscribed in 2008. The listing centres on welcoming dead relatives home with flower petals, candles and their favourite food: remembrance, not trick-or-treating.

Performance scholar Mathew Sandoval traces, in [*The Conversation* on 30 October 2023](https://theconversation.com/day-of-the-dead-is-taking-on-halloween-traditions-but-the-sacred-holiday-is-far-more-than-a-mexican-halloween-212686), how US Latinos began insisting the day was no "Mexican Halloween" once it went public there in the 1970s and 1980s. He also argues the two now blend. Send *Feliz Halloween* on the 31st, then shift to remembrance:

- "Que tus seres queridos te acompañen en el recuerdo estos días." (May your loved ones be with you in memory these days.)
- "Pienso en ti y en los tuyos este 2 de noviembre." (I'm thinking of you and yours this 2 November.)
- "Que la luz de las velas te traiga buenos recuerdos." (May the candlelight bring you good memories.)

## Putting your Spanish on a Halloween card

For one person, paste your Spanish into the [interactive Halloween card with photos and music](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween): a letter, up to six photos and a word they carve into the pumpkin, in about 5 minutes. Its closing question is editable up to 60 characters, so *¿Te quedas conmigo hasta el último susto?* fits.

For a voice they will recognise, the [premium cinematic Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note up to 60 seconds, up to 12 photos, a 3,000-character letter and an optional unlock time, in about 10 minutes. Both suit one recipient, not a party, and 38.5% of creators add a password before sharing.

For a partner abroad on the 31st, the [long-distance "I miss you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is built for distance rather than one night. It keeps working after Halloween ends.

## When to skip a Spanish Halloween message

Three situations call for restraint. The first is tied to 1–2 November.

- **Someone in mourning.** A pumpkin card beside a fresh altar reads as careless. Send a remembrance line, or call.
- **Households that skip Halloween.** Some religious families ignore 31 October; a plain good-night message is kinder.
- **You cannot check the Spanish.** Machine translation often mixes *tú* and *usted* in one sentence. Ask a native speaker, or keep to *¡Feliz Halloween!*

The templates' own interface is English; only your text will be Spanish. Pages average 11.1 views each, but that helps only someone who opens links, and an abuela with no smartphone deserves paper.

- Lara Bermejo, V., *Pragmalingüística* 30, December 2022 (abstract only).
- Moyna, M. I. et al., *International Journal of the Sociology of Language*, February 2026 (open access).
- UNESCO, "Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead", inscribed 2008.
- Sandoval, M., *The Conversation*, 30 October 2023.
